lessons.question: An assistant answers confidently and mentions your 40-page attachment. Does that prove it read every page?
options: Yes, a confident answer means it saw everything
Yes, if the answer mentions the attachment by name
No, it may have used only part of the material
lessons.explanation: A context window limits what a model can use in one request, and products may summarise or retrieve only some material. Ask for a specific source ID and check the passage yourself.

lessons.after: An assistant is the interface through which
lessons.question: Which of these systems is choosing its own next step?
options: One that picks between searching tickets or opening a policy, based on findings
One that always reads, checks fields, classifies, then queues a draft
A chat window where you type a question and get a reply
lessons.explanation: An agent selects its next action from available tools based on what it observes. A fixed sequence is a workflow, even if a model does one of the steps.

lessons.prompt: Where should each part of Harbour's reporting work live?

items.text: Spotting that one ticket mixes a visit change and an invoice query
Allowing a refund to be issued
Counting how many rows were excluded
Proposing a category for a vaguely worded request
Stopping drafts from being sent to customers

lessons.explanation: Fully specified arithmetic belongs in code, interpreting language suits a model, and authority must be enforced by the application. A more capable model does not remove these distinctions.

lessons.after: Start with the required output and the
lessons.prompt: Put the decision procedure in order, from first question to last resort.
steps: Name the required output and the cost of getting it wrong
Use a formula or lookup if it fully specifies the answer
For numerical predictions from labelled history, test a predictive model against a simple baseline
If language must be interpreted, try one bounded model call
Add an agent only when choosing the next tool is itself useful
lessons.explanation: Each step adds setup and review work, so you only move on when the simpler option cannot do the job.

lessons.prompt: An owner says, "I want AI to run support." What would you need pinned down before you could tell whether it worked?
lessons.answer: An input (one ticket), an output (a proposed category and review flag), an authority boundary (save a draft, never send) and a finish condition. Without these there is nothing concrete to evaluate.

lessons.after: The ten fictional Harbour timings total 120
lessons.question: One easy ticket took three minutes with AI help. What is the safest conclusion?
options: AI saves about nine minutes on every ticket
Very little, because one easy case does not represent next week's mix
Staff can now handle four times as many tickets
lessons.explanation: A real baseline needs representative cases, a defined start and end, and a record of rework. A single easy case cannot support a savings claim.

lessons.after: Rank opportunities using five questions: Is
lessons.prompt: Using the five questions, sort these ideas for a first project.

items.text: Drafting a weekly report from bounded files a manager already reviews
A rare, high-consequence decision with an impressive demo
Suggesting categories for frequent tickets, with drafts reviewed
A task where nobody can tell whether the output is right
A task needing data the team is not authorised to use

lessons.explanation: Good first candidates are frequent, have observable output, use authorised information, let mistakes be caught early, and have an owner for exceptions.

lessons.after: Choose weekly report preparation for Harbour
lessons.question: What does success mean for Harbour's report project?
options: Every ticket in the week is resolved automatically
Refunds are executed faster than before
The model writes the report without Maya seeing it
A draft with the right period, accepted totals, open data problems and evidence
lessons.explanation: Success is defined by checkable contents of the draft. Refund execution stays outside the project, and Maya's review remains part of the process.

lessons.prompt: An assistant gives the correct net total but explains it with the wrong exclusions. Would you accept its answer?
lessons.answer: Accept the number only after your own check, and mark the reasoning unsupported. A right answer for the wrong reason will fail when next week's data differs.

lessons.after: Draw the current process as receive, inspect
lessons.prompt: Put one Harbour support case through the current process, in order.
steps: A ticket arrives in the shared inbox
Staff check the details and required fields
Staff choose a category and whether review is needed
A draft reply is saved for review
The outcome and minutes taken are logged
lessons.explanation: These are receive, inspect, decide, act and record. Naming a responsible person for each stage shows where review and authority sit.

lessons.after: If a report is generated instantly but takes
lessons.question: Which comparison would be unfair?
options: A fully reviewed manual reply versus an AI draft nobody checked
Ten manual cases versus ten AI-assisted cases from the same mix
Both timed from ticket received to reviewed reply
lessons.explanation: Both sides must reach the same definition of complete. An unchecked draft has skipped work the manual process included.

lessons.prompt: Write your task boundary in one sentence. Could a stranger judge a result complete without asking what you meant?
lessons.answer: A strong boundary names the input, the output, what is excluded, and who reviews it. For example: given one week's files, draft the report with checked totals and evidence for Maya; no refunds or messages.
